Build a feature whose State has a home outside the component.

A detail view is easy to begin and easy to outgrow. As loading, editing, errors, and cleanup arrive, one component can become responsible for user interaction, rendering, and the rules that govern its data. This tutorial starts by giving the character feature a focused State boundary before those responsibilities become tangled.

Why this boundary matters

keeps Feature State and its pipeline in an Angular service, so the component can stay focused on display and temporary user interaction. It does not replace the component; it gives the component a clear, reactive State source to render.

Use this structure for

  • a profile, product, or record detail view
  • a selected item from a managed collection
  • a feature that will later add editing, loading, and validation

By the end of this chapter

You will have a typed, service-owned , initialized with character State and exposed to an Angular component as a read-only, reactive detail view.

Chapter 1 Starting Point

Start from an empty working directory. This chapter creates the Angular project and every file required for the first read path. The checked-in tutorial baseline uses Node.js 24 or newer, npm 11 or newer, and Angular 21. If your organization standardizes different supported versions, use a mutually compatible Angular and SDuX package set.

Files You Will Create or Change
  • star-wars-character.shape.ts and star-wars-character.constant.ts define the domain contract and seed data.
  • example.service.ts owns the FeatureCell and exposes its reactive snapshot.
  • app.config.ts registers the Vault and the feature; main.ts bootstraps the example.
  • The component, template, and stylesheet render the first committed character without calling SDuX APIs directly.
Ownership Rule for Every Chapter

Keep committed Feature State and all FeatureCell calls in the service. Keep selection, form controls, confirmation prompts, and display-only feedback in the component unless a later requirement explicitly makes that data shared Feature State.

Step 3: Define Feature State

↑ top

State is the feature-owned data that describes a feature at a specific moment. Defining State means deciding which values belong to the feature, assigning a type to each value, and identifying which properties are required.

In TypeScript, an interface captures those decisions as a compile-time contract for the and its consumers. This contract makes the expected State shape explicit, keeps State usage consistent, and allows TypeScript to identify missing properties and incompatible values during development. The interface defines the shape of State; it does not create or load a State value.

In , each declares State for a single Feature. This keeps the State definition focused on the data owned by that Feature instead of combining unrelated application data into one shared global store definition.

In this tutorial, the Feature and its State represent characters from the Star Wars universe.

Each character has an identifier, name, faction, and force-sensitive status. Keeping these fields in one focused State definition gives the , Pipeline, and Angular application a consistent representation of the character data.

Make the Change
  1. Create a new file named: star-wars-character.shape.ts

Global Store vs.

In a global store, all application data is combined into one shared State definition. This can lead to a large, complex State shape that is difficult to manage and maintain. In contrast, a defines State for a single Feature, keeping the State definition focused and manageable.

Step 6: Register the

↑ top

The provide() provider registers ExampleService with the application-scoped . Its descriptor assigns the unique star-wars-character key and supplies an initial character collection whose entries satisfy StarWarsCharacter. Registration establishes the contract for a typed collection before the Pipeline is activated or any State is rendered in the UI.

Registration Is Not Activation
  • provideVault() creates the application-level SDuX runtime.
  • provideFeatureCell() declares the unique key, State type, initial value, behaviors, and controllers available to this feature.
  • @FeatureCell() associates the service with that same key, and injectVault() gives the service its typed API.
  • initialize() starts the registered FeatureCell lifecycle. Configure fluent APIs before calling it.
Make the Change
  1. Create star-wars-character.constant.ts.
  2. Open app.config.ts.
  3. Import provide() and ExampleService.
  4. Add the provide() registration after provideVault().
  5. Assign the star-wars-character key and provide the initial character collection.

Step 7: Connect the Service to

↑ top

This is the step where the plain Angular service becomes an Feature service. The goal is straightforward: connect ExampleService to the registered so the service owns access to the typed feature State.

adds three pieces here: the @() decorator to associate the service with its key, injectVault() to access the typed API, and initialize() to activate the at runtime.

After this step, the component will no longer need to know anything about registration or initialization. It will read from the service's exposed state, while the service remains the only place that talks directly to .

Make the Change

Step 8: Display Character State

↑ top

This step narrows the tutorial to the UI-facing files that complete the first read path. The service boundary is already in place; now the component, template, and stylesheet turn that registered character collection into a visible detail view.

For , the important separation is simple: the component reads display-ready State, and the service owns the .

In this example, the component reads the service's reactive State, derives one displayed character, and passes only template-ready values to the view. The stylesheet is included here because later tutorial expansions reuse the same presentation base.

Make the Change
  1. Create example.component.ts in the same directory as the State definition.
  2. Create example.component.html in the same directory.
  3. Create example.component.scss in the same directory.
What to Look For
  • The component uses a computed Signal to project one displayed character from the service-owned collection State.
  • The template stays declarative and renders only controller state, not APIs.
  • The SCSS is larger than this single view requires because the same styling foundation is reused by the later tutorial steps.
New Symbols and Their Owners
  • characters is a component computed Signal that projects the service's committed collection.
  • The component injects ExampleService; it never injects or configures the FeatureCell directly.
  • The template reads component values only. The SCSS is reusable presentation scaffolding and has no State authority.

Step 9: Start the Application

↑ top

You are now ready to bootstrap the application with the ExampleComponent and view the first character from the registered collection.

Make the Change
  1. Open the main.ts file.
  2. Import ExampleComponent from ./app/example.component.
  3. Pass ExampleComponent as the root component in bootstrapApplication().
  4. Run npm start.
  5. Open http://localhost:4200 to confirm the character detail view renders.
Expected Result and Recovery
  • The page renders the first seeded character with its identifier, name, faction, and Force-sensitive value. No selection or edit controls are present yet.
  • If Angular reports that the service or FeatureCell cannot be resolved, compare the key in provideFeatureCell() with the key in @FeatureCell(), and confirm provideVault() appears first in the provider list.
  • If the page renders but no value appears, confirm the seed collection is passed as initialState and that the service calls initialize() after configuration.

Review the remaining supporting files as one connected reference. This final section gathers the seed data, registration config, and tests that complete the tutorial example.

By this point, the runtime path is already established. The focus here is on the remaining support files that make the example complete and verifiable.

The test files show how to verify the two critical responsibilities introduced in this tutorial. The service test confirms that the registered initializes with the expected collection State and exposes the correct Signal accessors. The component test confirms that the controller binds to that State and derives the single displayed character the template renders.

What This Final Reference Includes

  • The app config shows how the feature is registered with provide().

  • Together, these files turn the minimal read example into a complete tutorial slice you can reason about and extend.
Tutorial Data Boundary

The checked-in constant supplies deterministic teaching data. In a production feature, adapt an authoritative API or persistence result before submitting it through the service-owned FeatureCell; keep transport parsing and hydration ownership out of the component.
